newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG's ragtag rebels face African "dogs of war".
newsitem.headline: PNG's ragtag rebels face African "dogs of war".

text.p: A small parrot sits perched on the barrel of a military assault rifle held by a young man dressed in a baggy denim jacket. His friends-in-arms stand around him, staring curiously at the photographer.
Most of the barefoot crowd is dressed in shorts, with T-shirts or unbuttoned shirts. Few are armed with anything more powerful than a machete or axe.

This is the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA), which for the past nine years has not only held the Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) at bay, but at times driven them off their mountainous, jungle-clad South Pacific island.
Now these young men, led by an Australian-trained commander, Sam Kauona, face a more daunting enemy -- African mercenaries.
On the Papua New Guinea mainland, at a military training camp deep in the jungle accessible only by helicopter, some 40 mercenaries are training troops for an assault on Bougainville.

According to South-African based Executive Outcomes, which is supplying the mercenaries, its men are veterans from the South African Defence Force and the African National Congress -- an unlikely alliance of former enemies united by profit.
Executive Outcomes is Africa's best known private army. It has helped Angola and Sierre Leone fight rebel threats.
The mercenaries are skilled in small, forward deployment squads and have brought high-tech, infra-red surveillance and night vision equipment into Third-World PNG.
PNG Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan has said the A$36 million (US$27 million) mercenary contract includes equipment purchases.
Local media reports say the mercenaries will help PNG buy six Russian-made helicopters within the next two weeks.

PNG has four Australian-donated Iroquois helicopters, but Canberra prohibits their use as gunships. Two are operational on Bougainville, one has been in Australia for the past year undergoing an overhaul and the other is being repaired in PNG.
PNGDF Chief-of-Staff Colonel Jack Tuat will not comment on any helicopter purchases, but admits gunships "would make our job very, very much easier".

But Tuat does not discount the rebels, saying they have evolved into a credible force, motivated by the dream of independence. "Over the nine years they have got quite extensive experience in guerrilla fighting. They are credible enough for us to think twice before we do anything," Tuat told Reuters.

Tuat said there are 1,000 rebels, but admits it fluctuates. Other military sources in Port Moresby put the number closer to 300-500. "They join and leave as they deem necessary. It is very ad hoc but it seems to work," said one military source.
But the source said in-fighting often depleted rebel ranks.
"You have got these inter-regional, inter-tribal faction rivalries. It is a real melting pot," he said.
An unsuccessful PNGDF offensive last year put 1,600 troops on the island. There are now only 500 troops and police on Bougainville, with rebels still controlling most of the island.
Political analysts cite the ill-disciplined nature of the PNGDF on Bougainville and a lack of adequate arms as significant reasons behind the government's failure to end the conflict.
"They have had an unfortunate record of continuous failure in Bougainville," said Jim Griffin, emeritus professor of history at the University of PNG.
London-based Amnesty International has consistently reported human rights abuses, including executions and torture, by both troops and rebels.
The BRA boasts predominately homemade rifles, but success from its hit and run raids has seen it capture numerous high-powered military rifles, such as M16s and SLRs, said Tuat.
Australia fears PNG will use the mercenaries to stage a surgical strike at rebel leaders. Chan has said BRA leaders are the target, but the mercenaries will only be used as advisors.
British-based Sandline International, the middle men in the mercenary deal, rejects suggestions its men are hired killers.
But some analysts doubt the PNGDF can be trained to a level necessary to independently launch a strike on rebel leaders.
"It will be necesary, if this is their objective, to use these mercenaries to lead and bolster the PNGDF in its present state," said Griffin.
"The result of that will undoubtably be search and destroy, greater bloodshed, and possibly no success at all..."
